name: database-notebook
description: JavaScript, SQL, and Markdown can be centrally managed within a single notebook file. Includes a database manager supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite, Oracle, Redis, Memcached, AWS, Keycloak, Auth0, and MQTT. Use your saved connections as AI tools in GitHub Copilot Chat (Agent mode) -- list/test connections, inspect schemas, run queries and transactions, scan non-SQL resources (Redis, Memcache, MQTT, Keycloak, Auth0, AWS), and create or edit .dbn notebooks directly from chat. Features intuitive MQTT publish/subscribe tools and the ability to query payloads with SQLite.
author: l-v-yonsama <32474032+l-v-yonsama@users.noreply.github.com>

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_testConnection
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Performs a live network connectivity test against a specific named database connection saved in Database Notebook's DB Explorer, by actually attempting to connect right now. Use this tool whenever the user asks things like 'is connection X reachable/working/up?', 'can I connect to X?', 'test/check/verify/troubleshoot the X connection' for any connection managed by Database Notebook (.dbn files, MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server/SQLite/Oracle/Redis/etc.). This performs a real, live check -- do not answer from static analysis of files or guesses, call this tool to get the current, authoritative answer. Requires the exact saved connection name; if the given name doesn't match, the tool returns the list of valid connection names instead. If you don't already know the exact connection name -- e.g. the user described it indirectly, like 'the local MySQL connection' or 'the production database' -- call listDbConnections first to resolve it by name/dbType/environment/description rather than guessing the name.
languageModelTools.userDescription: Tests whether a saved Database Notebook connection can connect.

connectionName.description: The exact name of the connection as configured in Database Notebook's DB Explorer.

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_listConnections
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Lists the database connections configured in Database Notebook that are allowed for AI tool access: name, database/resource type, environment label (e.g. local/development/staging/production, if set), an optional free-text description of what the connection is for, and a short type-specific detail (e.g. which AWS services -- DynamoDB, S3, CloudWatch Logs, SQS, SES -- an AWS connection is configured for, the protocol for an MQTT connection, or whether a SQL connection (MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server/SQLite/Oracle) is marked read-only -- for SQL Server this is only a routing hint, not an enforced guarantee, so write attempts can still succeed there). No credentials are included. Use this when the user asks what connections exist, which databases/services they can use, what a given connection is configured for, which one is the local/dev/production one, or asks a question like 'which connection was it again?' before using another Database Notebook tool such as checking connectivity or running a query. A connection marked read-only will reject write/DDL statements (except the SQL Server hint-only case above) -- prefer it for read-heavy tasks and avoid it, or warn the user, before attempting writes.
languageModelTools.userDescription: Lists the Database Notebook connections available to AI tools.

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_getSchema
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Returns schema or resource information for a connection managed by Database Notebook, in a format appropriate to its type. For a SQL connection (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite, Oracle): the CREATE TABLE DDL (columns, types, primary/foreign keys, comments) for a table, or all tables -- optionally narrow with schemaName and/or tableName. For an AWS connection: the configured resources -- S3 bucket names, SQS queue names/URLs, CloudWatch log group names, and DynamoDB table key schemas (partition/sort key, attribute types, GSI/LSI counts) -- optionally narrow with serviceType and/or resourceName. For a Redis connection: each DB index and its key count. For a Memcache connection: key counts per cache tier (hot/warm/cold) and the configured servers. For a Keycloak connection: each realm with user/group counts -- optionally narrow with realmName. For an Auth0 connection: user/organization counts, plus organization/client lists where the connection is configured to retrieve them. For an MQTT connection: the configured topic subscriptions with QoS. All filters are optional and independent; omit any of them to get every match. Use this when the user asks about table/resource structure, columns, relationships, or before writing SQL/inspecting resources against a connection you haven't inspected yet. For searching/browsing individual records or keys within a resource (not just its structure/summary), use scanDbResource instead. If you don't already know the exact connection name -- e.g. the user described it indirectly, like 'the local MySQL connection' or 'the production database' -- call listDbConnections first to resolve it by name/dbType/environment/description rather than guessing the name.
languageModelTools.userDescription: Gets table structure (DDL) from a SQL connection, resource details from an AWS connection, or a summary (key counts, realms, topics, etc.) from a Redis/Memcache/Keycloak/Auth0/MQTT connection.

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_runQuery
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Runs a SQL statement against a SQL connection (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite, Oracle) managed by Database Notebook, or a PartiQL statement against an AWS connection configured for DynamoDB, and returns the results. Prefer read-only SELECT/EXPLAIN/SHOW statements. Write/DDL statements (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/CREATE/ALTER/DROP/etc.) will always require the user's explicit confirmation before running, and on SQL Server or DynamoDB connections every statement requires confirmation regardless of type. Not supported for other non-SQL connections (Redis, MQTT, other AWS resources like S3/SQS/CloudWatch, etc.) -- use scanDbResource to search those instead. To run multiple statements as one atomic transaction, use runDbTransaction instead of calling this tool repeatedly (DynamoDB connections are not supported by runDbTransaction). Use getDbSchema first if you don't already know the table structure. If you don't already know the exact connection name -- e.g. the user described it indirectly, like 'the local MySQL connection' or 'the production database' -- call listDbConnections first to resolve it by name/dbType/environment/description rather than guessing the name.
languageModelTools.userDescription: Runs a SQL query against a Database Notebook connection.

connectionName.description: The exact name of the connection as configured in Database Notebook's DB Explorer.

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_scanResource
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Searches/browses data in a non-SQL connection managed by Database Notebook (Redis, Memcache, Mqtt, Keycloak, Auth0, or AWS S3/SQS/CloudWatch Logs) using resource-specific scan parameters, since these connections cannot run SQL. Not supported for SQL connections (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite, Oracle) or AWS DynamoDB -- use runDbQuery for SQL connections. Set connectionName and fill in exactly ONE of the nested parameter objects matching the connection's type: redis, memcache, mqtt, awsS3, awsSqs, awsCloudWatchLogGroup, awsCloudWatchLogStream, keycloak, or auth0 -- each object's fields only apply to that connection type, do not mix fields from different objects. Call getDbSchema first if you don't know the connection's exact resource names (bucket/queue/log group/log stream names) or which AWS sub-resource it is, and call listDbConnections first if you don't know the exact connection name. Mqtt scanning requires the connection to already be connected and subscribed to the relevant topics via the MQTT panel -- it does not auto-connect, and returns an error telling you so if it isn't.

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_runTransaction
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Runs multiple SQL statements against a SQL connection (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite, Oracle) managed by Database Notebook as a single atomic transaction, in order, stopping at the first failure. Use this instead of calling runDbQuery repeatedly whenever the statements must all succeed or all be undone together (e.g. a sequence of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE across related tables). For a single statement, use runDbQuery instead. Choose transactionControlType carefully: 'rollbackOnError' (default, recommended) commits only if every statement succeeds and rolls back everything on any failure; 'alwaysCommit' commits whatever ran even after a failure, keeping partial writes -- use only when partial progress is acceptable; 'alwaysRollback' always rolls back even on full success, useful for a dry run. Not supported for non-SQL connections (Redis, Memcache, MQTT, Keycloak, Auth0, AWS) -- use scanDbResource for those. Every invocation always requires the user's explicit confirmation, showing every statement and the chosen transaction mode, before running -- this is not skipped even if every statement looks like a read. If you don't already know the exact connection name, call listDbConnections first, and use getDbSchema first if you don't already know the table structure.
languageModelTools.userDescription: Runs multiple SQL statements as one all-or-nothing transaction against a Database Notebook connection.

connectionName.description: The exact name of the connection as configured in Database Notebook's DB Explorer.

statements.description: The SQL statements to run in order, inside one transaction.

transactionControlType.description: How to commit/roll back. 'rollbackOnError' (default): commit only if all statements succeed. 'alwaysCommit': commit even after a failure (partial writes kept). 'alwaysRollback': always roll back, even on success (dry run).

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_createNotebook
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Creates a new Database Notebook (.dbn) file from a list of cells and opens it in the editor. Use this whenever the user asks to create/make/generate a notebook, save queries as a notebook, or put an analysis somewhere they can re-run it -- do not just print SQL/code in chat when the user wants a runnable notebook artifact. Provide notebookPath for a NEW file: this tool refuses to overwrite an existing file or an already-open notebook, so use editDbNotebook instead if one already exists there. Provide either cells (an ordered array of code/markup cells -- use this for mixed-language notebooks, markdown explanations, or per-cell connection/metadata overrides) or sqlText (a convenience that splits raw, possibly multi-statement SQL text into one SQL cell per statement, the same way Database Notebook's own "Create Notebook from SQL" command does). Every cell runs on its own independent, auto-committing connection: a "sql" cell's value must be exactly one statement (a PL/SQL block or procedure/function/trigger body counts as one statement despite its internal semicolons, but never join separate statements like two UPDATEs into one cell), and must never contain BEGIN/START TRANSACTION/COMMIT/ROLLBACK -- they're unnecessary and can error, since the cell commits automatically the instant it finishes running. Split multiple statements across multiple cells instead. Any cell that runs against a connection (sql, cwql, memcached, or an MQTT publish cell) needs a connectionName -- set it per-cell, or once via the top-level connectionName to apply it to every cell that needs one. Only connections enabled for AI tool use can be set; if you don't already know the exact connection name, call listDbConnections first, and call getDbSchema first if you need table/column names to write correct SQL. This tool only authors the notebook -- it never runs any cell itself.
languageModelTools.userDescription: Creates a new Database Notebook (.dbn) file from a list of cells or raw SQL, and opens it.

notebookPath.description: Where to save the new notebook: a path relative to the first workspace folder (e.g. "reports/monthly.dbn") or an absolute path. A ".dbn" extension is appended automatically if omitted. Fails if a file (or an already-open notebook) already exists at the resolved path -- use editDbNotebook to modify an existing notebook instead of calling this again.

connectionName.description: Optional default connection name applied to every generated cell that needs one (from sqlText, or any cells[] entry that omits its own metadata.connectionName). Must be a connection enabled for AI tool use; call listDbConnections first if you don't already know the exact name.

sqlText.description: Convenience alternative to cells: raw, possibly multi-statement SQL text. Split into one SQL code cell per statement the same way Database Notebook's own "Create Notebook from SQL" command splits it (on top-level semicolons, respecting quoted strings and comments). Do not include transaction-control statements (BEGIN/START TRANSACTION/COMMIT/ROLLBACK) -- each resulting cell auto-commits on its own connection, so they're unnecessary and would just become their own error-prone cell. Provide exactly one of cells or sqlText.

cells.description: Explicit ordered list of cells to create. Provide exactly one of cells or sqlText. Use this (not sqlText) for markup cells, non-SQL code cells, mixed-language notebooks, or when different cells need different connections/metadata.

"cwql": a CloudWatch Logs Insights query cell (also requires metadata.logGroupName). "memcached": a Memcache command cell. "javascript": a JS scripting cell. "json": a JSON value cell, or -- combined with metadata.publishParams -- an MQTT publish cell. "plaintext": a raw MQTT publish payload cell (also requires metadata.publishParams).

languageModelTools.name: database-notebook_editNotebook
languageModelTools.modelDescription: Applies one or more structural edits -- inserting, replacing, or deleting cells, or updating a single cell's metadata or source text -- to an EXISTING Database Notebook (.dbn) file, identified by notebookPath. Use this to modify a notebook the user is working on (e.g. "add a cell that...", "delete the second cell", "change the connection cell 3 uses", "fix the SQL in the last cell") instead of describing the change in chat. This tool never creates a notebook -- if notebookPath doesn't exist yet, call createDbNotebook instead. It always asks the user to confirm before making any change, showing every planned operation -- this is not skipped even for additive-looking operations, because an AI silently rewriting a file's content is a different trust situation than a human's own editor click. Provide operations as an ordered array; they are applied one at a time, in order, and cell index/range values for operation N refer to cell positions AFTER operations 1..N-1 in the SAME array have already been applied, not the notebook's original layout -- e.g. inserting 2 cells at index 3, then referencing index 3 or 4 in a later operation in the same call, refers to a cell you just inserted. Ranges are 0-based with an EXCLUSIVE end, like an array slice: {start:1,end:3} covers cells 1 and 2 only. Cells you insert or replace follow the same shape, connectionName rules, and one-statement-per-cell / no-transaction-control rules as createDbNotebook's cells (see its description for why) -- call listDbConnections first if you don't already know the exact, AI-enabled connection name. The same one-statement, no-BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK rule applies to a "sql" cell's text when replacing it via updateCellSource, even though that operation doesn't set language. If any single operation in the array is invalid (an out-of-range index, or a disallowed connectionName), the entire call fails with no changes applied -- fix the batch and call again rather than retrying operation by operation. Edits are left unsaved in the editor afterward, so the user has a final chance to review (or undo) before the change reaches disk.

operations.description: Ordered list of edit operations, applied one at a time in array order. Cell index/range values in operation N refer to cell positions AFTER operations 1..N-1 in THIS array have already been applied -- not the notebook's original layout. If any operation is invalid, none of the operations in this call are applied.

retain.description: Whether the broker should retain the published message.

updateCellSource.description: Replace one existing cell's full source text. Its kind, language, and metadata are unchanged. If the cell is a "sql" cell, the replacement text must still be exactly one statement (a PL/SQL block or procedure/function/trigger body counts as one statement) with no BEGIN/START TRANSACTION/COMMIT/ROLLBACK -- each cell auto-commits on its own connection.

cellIndex.description: 0-based index of the cell to update.

source.description: The cell's new full source text, entirely replacing its current content.

scripts.install:all: npm install && cd webview-ui && npm install
scripts.vscode:prepublish: npm run build:webview && npm run compile
scripts.pretest: npm run compile && npm run lint
